Chile's Law 16.744 makes employers insure their workers against work accidents, commuting
accidents and occupational diseases, with one of three private mutual insurers (ACHS, MUSEG, IST)
or the public Instituto de Seguridad Laboral (ISL). The Superintendencia de Seguridad Social
(SUSESO) publishes their statistics each year. This notebook uses the tables of SUSESO's 2014 to
2025 yearbooks. Read the module [README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md)
first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/cl-suseso-work-accidents/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name, ...) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           ...)
}

national <- read_module("tidy", "national.csv")
sectors <- read_module("tidy", "by_sector.csv")
regions <- read_module("tidy", "by_region.csv")
size <- read_module("tidy", "by_size.csv")
by_sex <- read_module("tidy", "by_sex.csv")
```

**Mutual insurers** are ACHS, MUSEG and IST together; **Total** adds the ISL. Accident rates are
published for the mutual insurers only; death rates for all insurers.

# Part 1. Fifteen years of work accidents

```{r long-view}
national |>
  filter(case_type == "Work accidents",
         (measure == "Accidents per 100 workers" & insurer == "Mutual insurers") |
           (measure == "Deaths per 100,000 workers" & insurer == "Total")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y") +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Work accidents in Chile (accident rate: mutual insurers; death rate: all insurers)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. How much did the work accident rate fall between 2010 and 2025? Did the death rate fall as
   steadily?
2. What happened in 2020? Why did the accident rate fall that year?
3. Give three reasons, other than safer work, why a reported accident rate might fall.

**Your answer:**



# Part 2. COVID-19 as an occupational disease

```{r covid}
national |>
  filter(measure == "Cases", insurer == "Mutual insurers",
         case_type %in% c("Occupational diseases", "Occupational diseases (excluding COVID-19)")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = case_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Occupational diseases, mutual insurers", x = NULL, y = "Cases", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Questions**

1. How many occupational diseases did the mutual insurers accept each year before 2020, and in
   2020 to 2023? What explains the jump?
2. The 2025 yearbook leaves COVID-19 out. Using the two series for 2021 to 2024, roughly how many
   of the cases in 2022 were COVID-19?
3. Should a disease caught from the public, such as COVID-19 in a health worker, count as an
   occupational disease? What would you need to know about a case to decide?

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Commuting accidents and sex

```{r commuting}
by_sex |>
  filter(by == "Insurer", insurer == "Total", year == 2025, measure == "Cases",
         sex %in% c("Female", "Male")) |>
  select(case_type, sex, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(female_share = round(Female / (Female + Male), 2))
```

**Questions**

1. What share of work accidents, commuting accidents and occupational diseases happened to women
   in 2025?
2. Women had more commuting accidents than men, but far fewer work accidents. Suggest reasons,
   about the jobs men and women do and about how they travel.
3. Chile compensates commuting accidents as work-related. Who can prevent them?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Sectors

```{r sectors}
sectors |>
  filter(year %in% 2023:2025, measure == "Deaths per 100,000 workers", case_type == "Work accidents",
         insurer == "Total", sector != "Total") |>
  group_by(sector) |>
  summarise(mean_2023_2025 = round(mean(value), 1), years = n()) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_2023_2025, fct_reorder(sector, mean_2023_2025))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Deaths from work accidents per 100,000 workers, mean of 2023 to 2025",
       x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which sectors have the highest death rates? Name the main hazards behind deaths in two of
   them.
2. Why does this chunk average three years instead of showing one?

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. Regions

```{r regions}
regions |>
  filter(year == 2024, insurer == "Mutual insurers", region != "Total",
         measure %in% c("Protected workers", "Cases", "Deaths"),
         is.na(case_type) | case_type == "Work accidents") |>
  select(region, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  filter(!is.na(`Protected workers`)) |>
  mutate(accidents_per_100 = round(100 * Cases / `Protected workers`, 2),
         deaths_per_100000 = round(1e5 * Deaths / `Protected workers`, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths_per_100000))
```

**Questions**

1. Which regions have the highest death rates in 2024? Which have the most deaths? Are they the
   same regions?
2. The northern regions (Antofagasta, Atacama, Tarapacá) are mining regions. Do their rates of
   accidents and deaths look like those of the mining sector in Part 4?
3. A region with few protected workers can have a high rate from one or two deaths. How would
   you judge whether a region's high rate is real?
